Your Excellency, Doctor Rahman, president of the eight first session of the United Nations General Assembly Your Majesties Excellencies, heads of State and Government, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. António Guterres, distinguished delegates.

Ladies and gentlemen I congratulate you, Doctor Rahman, on your election as president of the eight first session of the General Assembly Zimbabwe's confident that under your able leadership, the Assembly will advance meaningful transformation under the theme Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation a United Nations that delivers for all.
You may count on Zimbabwe's full support.
I wish to thank Miss Annalena Baerbock for her effective leadership of the 80th session and their contribution to the UN aid reform process.
REF1
Zimbabwe also pays tribute to Mr. António Guterres in his final general debate as Secretary general.
We commend his defense of multilateralism as well as efforts to advance dialogue for conflict prevention and resolution, sustainable development and the pact for the future.

These experiences reveal a common truth.
Humanity's challenges are increasingly interconnected, and no nation can overcome them alone.
The trust deficit among nations has continued to erode the gains that cooperation fostered within the United Nations system.
We must therefore choose between purposeful reform or unmitigated repression.
Trust will be restored when conflicts are prevented.
International law is applied equally.
PSJ5
Development commitments are fulfilled, and all nations are fairly represented in global institutions.
Multilateralism is a crucial equalizer.
It ensures that all have an equal voice under international law, and an equal role in shaping our shared future.

Undoubtedly, the charter remains our common compass sovereign equality, political independence, territorial integrity, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and international cooperation must be applied universally, not selectively.
International law cannot be a shield for some and a sword against others.
The United Nations has a sacred duty to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.
Our experience in southern Africa has taught us that dialogue is a shared fortitude and not a weakness.
In the African tradition, the meeting place is not where courage is abandoned.
It is where wisdom is summoned.
Lessons can be drawn from the heritage based approaches to peace building and conflict resolution from communities across the world, including within Africa.
PSJ2

Military action may alter the battlefield, but durable peace is built through inclusive political processes that restore confidence, address grievances and allow affected communities to shape their socioeconomic and political destinies.

Mr. president, Zimbabwe's grateful for the confidence placed in us through our election to the Security Council for the 2027 to 2028 term, my country will assume this responsibility in January 2027 with humility, independency and a readiness to serve, guided by our foreign policy of being a friend to all and an enemy to none.
Accordingly, my country will prioritize for priorities in the Council.
Firstly, the promotion of preventive diplomacy, mediation, a peaceful dispute resolution while tackling the underlying causes of insecurity.
Secondly, we shall advocate for the strengthening of cooperation between the United Nations and the regional organizations such as the African Union and its Peace and Security Council.
In this respect, we call for the full implementation of resolution 2719 to ensure predictable, adequate and sustainable financing for authorized African Union led peace support operations.

Thirdly, our nation believes that our rich heritage and natural resource endowments must advance industrialization, modernization and the green agenda for the prosperity of all and not to finance conflict As such, Zimbabwe shall support Africa silencing the guns agenda and strong action against terrorism, organized crime, illicit arms flows, and illegal resource trafficking.

Zimbabwe is continuously strengthening its capacity to mobilise domestic resources, enhance public financial management and foster a favourable environment for productive investment and our National Vision 2030.
We are strengthening the important linkage between mining and agriculture, which is driving growth in Zimbabwe's manufacturing sector.

Through our rural industrialisation agenda and the Invest Rural policy, we are directing investment towards rural infrastructure, manufacturing hubs and agro processing facilities.
More women and youth continue to enter value chain industries for both our local and regional markets.
As droughts, floods and declining productivity threaten water, food and energy security.

Harnessing emerging technologies for national development is a key priority for our industrialisation agenda.

The next holder of the office should be an impartial custodian of the charter.
An independent voice for peace, a bridge builder among member states, and an advocate for those whose voices seldom reach these halls.
The process should be transparent, inclusive and guided by merit.
Equitable geographical representation and gender equality.
Above all, the next Secretary-General must bring the United Nations closer to the people.
The charter begins with we, the peoples of the United Nations.
Those words should guide how the organization listens, how it communicates, and how it measures the success.
In conclusion, Zimbabwe will assume its role in the Security Council.
Mindful that membership is not a badge of honor, but a commitment to serve the comity of nations.

We will serve with balance and integrity, defend the sovereign equality of states, advance Africa's priorities and work constructively with all regions Let this 81st decision be recorded as the session that closed the gap between the promises of the charter and the realities of the daily life, Zimbabwe is ready to play its part in building the future we all want.
